sentences.text: Utahraptor stands as the largest known member of the dromaeosaurid family, reaching lengths of approximately 6 to 7 meters and weighing around 500 kilograms.
The genus name Utahraptor references Utah, the discovery site, while the specific name ostrommaysi honors John Ostrom and Chris Mays for their contributions to dromaeosaur research.
Originally named U. spielbergi, the species was renamed shortly before publication to avoid legal threats from Universal Studios regarding the use of the word "Jurassic".
The genus was formally described in 1993 by James Kirkland and colleagues based on fossils unearthed from the Cedar Mountain Formation in Utah.
Initial specimens were found in 1975 by Jim Jensen at the Dalton Wells Quarry, with further remains uncovered in 1991 by Kirkland, Gaston, and Burge at the Gaston Quarry.
As a carnivore, this predator hunted animals such as ankylosaurs and iguanodonts within the Cedar Mountain Formation ecosystem.
Physiological evidence suggests Utahraptor functioned as an ambush predator, a strategy distinct from the pursuit tactics seen in other dromaeosaurs.
Shortened chevrons and prezygapophyses in the tail likely increased flexibility compared to many other members of the group.
Fossil remains of individuals of various ages suggest the species was gregarious and practiced some form of post-nestling care.
Utahraptor is classified as a genus of large theropod dinosaur belonging to the family Dromaeosauridae, commonly known as raptors.
James Kirkland and colleagues initially placed the species in the subfamily Dromaeosaurinae, which is now part of the clade Eudromaeosauria.
This animal lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically from the Berriasian to the Valanginian stages, in the lower part of the Cedar Mountain Formation's Yellow Cat Member.

Thomas R. Holtz estimated its existence between 130 and 125 million years ago, though Joeckel and colleagues (2019) concluded the Yellow Cat Member is older than previous estimations using radiometric dating.
In 2019, Costa and David criticized the emended name ostrommaysorum, arguing it lacks clear justification or explanation.
A 2019 analysis suggested Utahraptor might belong to a clade outside Dromaeosaurinae, though it could be moved to Dromaeosaurinae or Velociraptorinae with minor changes.

It remains unclear whether all individuals in a specific fossil block were mired simultaneously or one by one, and further examination suggests the number of remains may be double the previously assumed amount.
